subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Thyroid Disorders: Congenital Hypothyroidism and Cretinism

steps.tx: Inadequate thyroid hormone biosynthesis in utero or early infancy impairs critical neurodevelopment and linear skeletal growth. The most common preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide is **congenital hypothyroidism in infants**, occurring in one in two thousand to three thousand live births. Thyroid dysgenesis accounts for eighty-five percent of cases, comprising thyroid gland ectopia (lingual or sublingual thyroid), complete agenesis (athyreosis), or gland hypoplasia.
steps.say: Congenital hypothyroidism is the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability, affecting one in three thousand newborns. Thyroid ectopia and agenesis cause eighty-five percent of cases.

vis.alt: Clinical photograph of an infant with congenital hypothyroidism displaying macroglossia, umbilical hernia, and coarse facial features.
vis.caption: Characteristic clinical appearance of infant with untreated congenital hypothyroidism demonstrating macroglossia and distension. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Universal newborn screening detects biochemical thyroid deficiency prior to the onset of irreversible neurological injury. Performing **newborn thyroid-stimulating hormone screening** utilizing dried blood spots collected on filter paper (Guthrie card) between forty-eight and seventy-two hours of life identifies elevated TSH above twenty to forty milliunits per litre. Testing before forty-eight hours must be interpreted cautiously due to the physiological neonatal TSH surge.
steps.say: Universal newborn screening measures TSH from heel-prick dried blood spots at forty-eight to seventy-two hours of life. Testing before forty-eight hours captures the physiological TSH surge.

left.title: Screening Protocol Specifics
points: Heel-prick capillary blood on filter paper (Guthrie card)
Optimal collection timing: 48 to 72 hours of life
Primary TSH screening with backup free T4 measurement
TSH >20-40 mIU/L prompts immediate confirmatory venous testing

right.title: Physiological Neonatal TSH Surge
points: Cold exposure at delivery triggers acute pituitary TSH surge
TSH peaks at 60-80 mIU/L within 30 minutes of birth
Spontaneously declines to normal (<10 mIU/L) by 48 hours
Early sampling (<48 hours) yields high false-positive rates

steps.tx: Clinical manifestations in the immediate neonatal period are subtle and easily missed due to protective transplacental maternal thyroxine. The earliest clinical clues in **early congenital hypothyroidism signs** include prolonged unconjugated neonatal jaundice lasting beyond two weeks, large anterior and posterior fontanelles (posterior fontanelle open wider than 0.5 cm), lethargy, poor suckling, hypothermia, cold mottled skin, and persistent neonatal constipation.
steps.say: Early signs are subtle, including prolonged neonatal jaundice beyond two weeks, wide fontanelles, hypothermia, and constipation. Maternal thyroxine masks early symptoms.

rows: Large anterior fontanelle; open posterior fontanelle
Hypotonia of abdominal wall rectus musculature
Myxoedematous infiltration of vocal cords and brain
Immediate serum TSH and free T4 assays

steps.tx: Delayed diagnosis beyond the first two to three months of life leads to permanent irreversible neurocognitive damage. The severe untreated syndrome known as **endemic or sporadic cretinism** is characterized by profound intellectual disability, severe stunted disproportionate dwarfism, coarse puffy facial features with a broad depressed nasal bridge, marked macroglossia protruding from the mouth, myxedematous dry doughy skin, and an umbilical hernia.
steps.say: Untreated congenital hypothyroidism leads to cretinism, characterized by profound intellectual disability, dwarfism, coarse facies, macroglossia, and umbilical hernia.

left.title: Neurological Cretinism Features
points: Profound permanent mental retardation (IQ <50)
Sensorineural bilateral deafness and deaf-mutism
Spastic diplegia or quadriplegia with hyperreflexia
Severe motor clumsiness and dystonic posture

right.title: Myxedematous Cretinism Features
points: Severe growth failure (disproportionate dwarfism)
Coarse thickened facial features with periorbital puffiness
Huge protruding tongue (macroglossia) causing airway noise
Dry, cool, thickened scaly skin with carotenemia

steps.tx: Radiographic examination demonstrates delayed epiphyseal maturation and characteristic disordered chondro-osseous ossification. Knee and foot radiographs in neonates evaluate the **absence of distal femoral epiphyses**, normally present in term infants by thirty-six to thirty-seven weeks of gestation, indicating intrauterine hypothyroidism. Later skeletal manifestations include epiphyseal dysgenesis, where ossification centers appear fragmented, stippled, and irregular like a burst sponge.
steps.say: Absence of the distal femoral epiphysis at birth indicates intrauterine hypothyroidism. Later radiographs show fragmented, stippled epiphyseal dysgenesis.

rows: Plain radiograph of the neonatal knee
Failure of ossification center to appear
Plain radiograph of the neonatal knee
Normally present at birth in term infants
Beaking of L1 or L2 vertebral bodies

steps.tx: Immediate oral levothyroxine replacement therapy initiated within the first two weeks of life ensures completely normal neurocognitive development. Standard dosing for **oral levothyroxine in congenital hypothyroidism** is ten to fifteen micrograms per kilogram per day administered once daily on an empty stomach. The therapeutic goal is rapid normalization of serum free T4 within one to two weeks and normalization of TSH within two to four weeks.
steps.say: Start oral levothyroxine at ten to fifteen micrograms per kilogram daily within two weeks of birth. Rapid normalization of free T4 within one to two weeks preserves intellectual potential.

left.title: Levothyroxine Administration Rules
points: Dose: 10 to 15 mcg/kg/day as single morning dose
Crush tablet in a small spoon with water or breast milk
Administer on an empty stomach 30 minutes before feeding
Never mix with soy formula, iron, or calcium supplements

right.title: Monitoring Targets & Timelines
points: Free T4 target: upper half of normal range (>1.5 ng/dL)
Serum TSH target: normalized between 0.5 and 2.0 mIU/L
Check TSH and free T4 every 1 to 2 months in the first year
Check every 2 to 3 months between ages 1 and 3 years

steps.tx: Autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis represents the leading cause of acquired thyroid failure in older children and adolescents. Typically emerging during puberty with a strong female predominance, **juvenile Hashimoto thyroiditis** results from autoimmune destruction by anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin autoantibodies. Children present with firm, painless, diffuse goitre, declining growth velocity crossing height percentiles, weight gain, constipation, and lethargy.
steps.say: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the commonest cause of acquired hypothyroidism in older children, caused by anti-TPO antibodies. It causes growth deceleration and a firm goitre.

rows: At birth or detected on newborn screen
Severe irreversible mental retardation if untreated
Normal IQ; mild sluggishness & poor school performance
Brain myelination complete by 2 to 3 years
Severe dwarfism with delayed bone age
Severe growth arrest with delayed bone age
Growth catch-up is dramatic on levothyroxine

steps.tx: Growth deceleration in the presence of preserved or increased weight gain represents the hallmark endocrine signature of childhood hypothyroidism. Children with **growth arrest in juvenile hypothyroidism** demonstrate dramatic flattening of linear height curves while weight continues along higher percentiles, resulting in an overweight, short child. Following levothyroxine replacement, profound catch-up growth occurs, restoring the child toward their genetic mid-parental target height.
steps.say: Falling height percentiles combined with rising weight percentiles indicate juvenile hypothyroidism. Levothyroxine therapy initiates dramatic catch-up growth.

left.title: Clinical Hallmark Presentation
points: Height velocity drops precipitously (<4 cm/year)
Relative weight gain or mild obesity
Delayed bone age significantly behind chronological age
Delayed dental eruption and delayed pubertal onset

right.title: Laboratory & Ultrasound Confirmation
points: Markedly elevated serum TSH with low free T4
Positive anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies
Ultrasound shows heterogeneous, hypoechoic thyroid
Levothyroxine replacement at 2 to 3 mcg/kg/day
